BIBLIOGRAPHY ................................................................................................................................................. 43 “Manufacturing full-scale high gradient copper accelerators: Electron beam welding and allied processes” Prepared for the U.S. Department of Energy ARDAP program A. Structure design and manufacturing A.1 Conventional Brazed, disk-type NCRF Accelerating Structures Fabrication of conventional, brazed NRCF accelerating structures is proceed via the following steps: 1. Procurement of accelerator grade copper1 2. Machining: 1.1. Rough machining of components from stock material, 1.2. (Optional) Stress relieving of components (500C/1hr in vacuum), 1.3. Precision machining of RF and positioning features. 2. Mechanical inspection for form and finish. 3. (Optional) Clamped cold testing. 4. Chemical cleaning of components. 5. Brazing of components into sub-assembly at T [oC] : Example: copper waveguide onto stainless steel 1 flange; cells into cell stack. 5.1. Inspection of sub-assemblies: mechanical, hermeticity, visual. 6. Post-braze machining of sub-assembly: Example: water cooling channels, waveguide to cell stack interface. 7. Brazing of sub-assembly components at temperature T < T : Example: cooling channels onto cell stack. 2 1 8. Final auxiliary joining: аttached target/gun/vacuum flanges and water cooling via TIG welding and/or mechanical fastening. It is important to mention that step 2: machining, often involves multiple different machining setups as well as the potential for using different machining equipment for each setup, with an example being rough machining on a low-precision milling machining and precision machining on a high-precision hybrid lathe with milling capabilities machine. Another item to note is the degree of mechanical inspection needed depends significantly on the complexity of the part, as well as whether or not it is a first article. In terms of chemical cleaning needed for NCRF AS, there are some differences in processes used, with some manufacturers only performing ultrasonic cleaning in a mild detergent, while others perform a combination of ultrasonic cleaning as well as 1-2µm of material removal via isotropic chemical etching. This difference is based on the target gradients and the machining technologies utilized, as low gradient AS do not require as pristine surface quality and ultra-precise machining technologies typically do not impart high levels of foreign material contamination. Brazing is done either in a hydrogen or vacuum atmosphere, again with some differences in technology used depending on provider and application. Roughly speaking, hydrogen brazing is historically more common and there are arguments to be made regarding improved cleanliness. Unfortunately, due to the safety challenges associated with hydrogen gas, it is an increasingly difficult to source process technology.
